steps.tx: The autoimmune condition **thyroid eye disease** is an inflammatory orbitopathy of Graves disease driven by shared antigen reactivity against both the TSH receptor and the **IGF-1 receptor** co-expressed on orbital fibroblasts. Tobacco **smoking** represents the most potent modifiable environmental risk factor, conferring a multi-fold increase in orbitopathy incidence and refractory progression. Strict smoking cessation is mandatory in all patients.
steps.say: Thyroid eye disease is an autoimmune orbitopathy driven by shared antibodies directed against TSH and IGF-1 receptors on orbital fibroblasts. Tobacco smoking is the most important modifiable risk factor, multiplying the risk of severe disease. Complete cessation of smoking is mandatory.

vis.caption: Orbital CT and pathology demonstrating retro-orbital expansion in Graves orbitopathy. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Disease activity is systematically assessed using the 7-item **clinical activity score** (**CAS**), where a score of 3 or higher indicates active inflammatory disease eligible for immunosuppression. Severity is categorized as mild, moderate-to-severe, or sight-threatening. Sight-threatening disease is defined by compressive **dysthyroid optic neuropathy** or corneal breakdown with ulceration, requiring emergent inpatient hospitalization and immediate intervention.
steps.say: Disease activity is graded using the clinical activity score, where a score of three or higher defines active inflammatory orbitopathy. Severity is classified into mild, moderate-to-severe, or sight-threatening stages. Sight-threatening disease presents as dysthyroid optic neuropathy or corneal breakdown requiring emergency admission.

rows: Minor lid retraction (<2 mm), mild soft-tissue signs
Lid retraction >=2 mm, proptosis >=3 mm, diplopia
Dysthyroid optic neuropathy or corneal ulceration
High-dose IV steroids, emergency orbital decompression

steps.tx: Eyelid retraction producing **lid lag** and stare can occur in any thyrotoxicosis due to heightened sympathetic stimulation of Muller muscle. In contrast, true extrathyroidal **proptosis**, restrictive diplopia, and chemosis are specific to thyroid eye disease itself. Pathological enlargement of extraocular muscles follows a predictable pattern, with the **inferior rectus** being the muscle most frequently involved, followed by the medial rectus.
steps.say: Sympathetic overactivity causes lid lag and stare in any thyrotoxic state. In contrast, true proptosis and restrictive strabismus are specific to thyroid eye disease. The inferior rectus muscle is most commonly involved, followed by the medial and superior rectus muscles.

left.title: Sympathetic Thyrotoxic Signs
points: Upper eyelid retraction and lid lag
Caused by adrenergic hyperstimulation of Muller muscle
Present in any form of severe thyrotoxicosis
Rapidly resolves with beta-blockers or euthyroidism

right.title: Specific Orbitopathy Signs
points: True proptosis (exophthalmos) measured by Hertel
Restricted ocular motility with diplopia
Inferior rectus is most commonly enlarged muscle
Driven by autoimmune glycosaminoglycan accumulation

steps.tx: For patients with mild active thyroid eye disease, oral **selenium** supplementation at a dose of **100** mcg twice daily for **6** months significantly improves ocular quality of life and delays disease progression in selenium-insufficient populations. This nutritional intervention is combined with artificial tear lubricants, ocular ointments, sunglasses, and absolute smoking cessation to maintain corneal epithelial integrity and prevent exposure keratitis.
steps.say: In mild active thyroid eye disease, oral selenium at one hundred micrograms twice daily for six months improves outcomes and reduces progression in selenium-deficient populations. This is combined with ocular lubricants, eye protection, and smoking cessation.

rows: 100 mcg orally twice daily for 6 months
Mild active disease in selenium-deficient areas

steps.tx: For moderate-to-severe active disease, the evidence-based first-line regimen utilizes intravenous **methylprednisolone** pulses: **500** mg weekly for **6** weeks, followed by **250** mg weekly for **6** weeks, delivering a cumulative total of 4.5 grams. Clinicians must strictly ensure that the cumulative glucocorticoid dose stays below **8** grams, because higher doses substantially increase the risk of acute hepatic necrosis and liver failure.
steps.say: Moderate-to-severe active disease is treated with intravenous methylprednisolone pulses of five hundred milligrams weekly for six weeks, followed by two hundred and fifty milligrams weekly for six weeks. The total cumulative steroid dose must remain under eight grams to prevent severe acute hepatic injury.

left.title: EUGOGO Pulse Regimen
points: 500 mg IV weekly for first 6 weeks
250 mg IV weekly for subsequent 6 weeks
Total cumulative dose: 4.5 grams methylprednisolone
Significantly superior to oral daily prednisolone

right.title: Glucocorticoid Safety Gate
points: Strict cumulative upper ceiling of 8 grams
Doses >8 g linked to fulminant hepatic necrosis
Baseline screening for viral hepatitis B and C
Monitor liver transaminases and serum glucose weekly

steps.tx: The monoclonal antibody **teprotumumab** binds specifically to the **IGF-1 receptor**, blocking its physical cross-talk with the TSH receptor. In randomized clinical trials in active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease, teprotumumab produced dramatic improvements, reducing **proptosis** by more than 2 to 3 mm and resolving diplopia. Clinicians must carefully monitor patients for **hyperglycemia**, especially in those with pre-existing diabetes, alongside audiometric screening for hearing loss.
steps.say: Teprotumumab is a targeted monoclonal antibody against the IGF-1 receptor that significantly reduces proptosis and diplopia in moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease. Serum glucose must be monitored closely because hyperglycemia is a frequent adverse effect, especially in patients with diabetes.

vis.caption: Orbital fibroblast activation, extraocular muscle enlargement, and proptosis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Sight-threatening **dysthyroid optic neuropathy** is caused by mechanical apical compression of the optic nerve by enlarged extraocular muscle bellies. Emergency treatment begins with immediate high-dose intravenous glucocorticoid pulses (500 to 1000 mg methylprednisolone daily for 3 days). If visual acuity or colour vision fails to improve within 1 to 2 weeks, urgent surgical **orbital decompression** is mandatory to avert permanent optic atrophy and blindness.
steps.say: Dysthyroid optic neuropathy represents an emergency caused by apical optic nerve compression. Management begins with immediate high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone. If vision does not improve within one to two weeks, urgent surgical orbital decompression is required to prevent permanent blindness.

left.title: Apical Compressive Neuropathy
points: Crowding of orbital apex by muscle bellies
Impaired colour vision, visual field defects
Relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD)
Optic disc swelling or early pallor

right.title: Urgent Decompression Protocol
points: Initial pulse IV methylprednisolone (0.5 to 1 g/day)
Re-evaluate visual acuity within 1 to 2 weeks
Urgent medial and floor bony decompression if refractory
Emergency intervention rather than delayed clinic review

steps.tx: Administration of **radioiodine** can worsen active thyroid eye disease by releasing thyroidal antigens and exacerbating autoimmune reactivity. Achieving and maintaining stable **euthyroidism** is paramount, because both hypothyroidism and persistent hyperthyroidism worsen orbital inflammation. When radioiodine is administered to patients with mild pre-existing orbitopathy or high-risk features like smoking, concomitant oral glucocorticoid prophylaxis with prednisolone (0.3 to 0.5 mg/kg) is mandatory.
steps.say: Radioactive iodine therapy can aggravate active thyroid eye disease by releasing autoantigens. Maintaining stable euthyroidism is critical because both hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism worsen orbitopathy. Prophylactic oral glucocorticoid cover should be given whenever radioiodine is administered to patients at risk.

rows: Radioiodine is contraindicated; choose ATD or surgery
Oral prednisolone (0.3 to 0.5 mg/kg) tapered over 3 months
Avoid post-radioiodine hypothyroidism with prompt thyroxine
